subject: science
intro: Ms. Johnson here. Let's plan a lesson where students become detectives, using evidence that continents move.

beats.narration: Framing it as detective work makes students look at the evidence closely.
This standard is about analyzing evidence from fossils, rocks, and seafloor features for past plate motions.
Claim, evidence, reasoning is built right into the objective.
beats.text: Students will be able to analyze fossil, rock, and landform evidence to support the claim that continents have moved over time.

beats.narration: They discover the fit themselves, just like Wegener did.
beats.text: Give each group paper continents to fit together like a puzzle. "What do you notice?"

beats.narration: The history shows science as a process of argument and new evidence.
beats.text: Present Wegener's evidence: matching fossils (Mesosaurus), matching rock layers, and glacier scratches in tropical areas. Explain why his idea was rejected until seafloor spreading evidence arrived.

beats.narration: The CER paragraph makes their argument concrete and gradable.
beats.text: Groups get evidence cards and map where each fossil or rock type is found on their puzzle continents, then write a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph.

beats.narration: This checks both the evidence and the reasoning.
beats.text: Name two pieces of evidence that continents were once connected and explain how each supports the claim.

outro: Puzzle, history, evidence, argument. Your turn.
